title: the Shiva Purana (selections)
hook: three brothers ask for three flying cities that can fall to only one arrow, and the whole world becomes Shiva's chariot

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Shiva Purana, a mother fainted at the groom, Parvati chose no one else, and Shiva showed a gentler face. Whom did you look at again? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-three.
screen: `LOOK AGAIN. SHOW A GENTLER SIDE.` · `TODAY: THREE CITIES.`

segments.voice: Every contract has a clause somebody hopes nobody will read. Three brothers in the Shiva Purana write theirs very carefully. They are the sons of Taraka, the demon whose boon sent the gods looking for a son of Shiva. With the marriage done, that son, Kartikeya, has defeated their father. Now the brothers go to the forest and practice tapas until Brahma, the creator, appears and offers them a boon. They ask for the obvious thing: never to die. Brahma says no. Nobody gets that. So they think again, and they ask for something cleverer.
screen: `THE SONS OF TARAKA.` → `NEVER TO DIE? NO.` → `SOMETHING CLEVERER.`

segments.voice: They ask for three cities. Maya, the great builder of the demons, makes them: one of gold in the heavens, one of silver in the sky, one of iron on the earth. And here's the clause. The cities can be destroyed only when the three come into line, which happens only rarely, and only by a single arrow. Three cities, one shot, one narrow moment. It sounds like the same thing as never dying, with better paperwork. For a long time the brothers flourish, and then they turn on the gods, and the gods come to Shiva. Now watch how the Shiva Purana builds the answer. Shiva needs a chariot, so the gods make one out of the world itself. The earth becomes the chariot. The sun and the moon become its wheels. Brahma takes the reins. The Vedas are the horses. A mountain is the bow, and Vishnu himself becomes the arrow. Everything has to come together for this one shot. And when the three cities slide into line, Shiva looses the arrow, and all three burn at once. Some tellings say he barely needed it: he smiled, and the cities caught fire. That's why one of his names is Tripurantaka, the ender of the three cities. Two things to carry out of it. First, the brothers' clause. They built their safety on a condition, and the condition was the crack. Nothing built can be made un-endable, however careful the wording. Second, the chariot. To meet that one moment, the whole world had to line up behind one arrow. On an ordinary Tuesday, a person can be three cities drifting in three directions: one part at work, one part on the phone, one part somewhere else entirely. Once in a while, everything lines up. That's when a single act goes all the way through.
screen: `THREE CITIES: GOLD, SILVER, IRON.` · `ONLY ONE ARROW, ONLY WHEN THEY ALIGN.` · `THE WHOLE WORLD BECOMES THE CHARIOT.` · `TRIPURANTAKA, ENDER OF THE THREE CITIES.` · then, large: `WHEN EVERYTHING LINES UP, ONE ACT GOES THROUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring the three cities into line. Settle, and let the breath slow. Notice where your attention is scattered right now: a bit in the body, a bit in something you have to do later, a bit in something that already happened. Don't scold any of it. Just gather it, one piece at a time, onto the breath, the way the cities drift slowly into a row. When it's gathered, even for a moment, choose one small thing you'll do today, and hold it there, aimed and steady. If you pray, you can say Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, as the breath goes out. The bell holds the time.
The Shiva Purana. Today's selection: three flying cities, one arrow, and a chariot made of the whole world. Shiva is Tripurantaka, ender of the three cities.
Your line: the Shiva Purana, in selections. Today, do one task with everything lined up behind it: phone away, nothing else open, one arrow. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Shiva as Tripurantaka, the destroyer of the three cities, is retold in the Shiva Purana and shown in temple sculpture with his bow drawn; the story is recited and sung in Shaiva worship.

fork.setup: you're one of Taraka's sons. Brahma has just refused to make you immortal. what do you ask for instead?
options: a vast army that can never lose.
three cities that can fall only to one arrow, only when they align.
fork.reveal: they ask for the three cities, a clause that sounds like never dying. the condition becomes the crack: Shiva's one arrow burns all three.

original.note: Sanskrit: Tripurantaka, the ender of the three cities, a name of Shiva from this story.

trapdoor: what you thought: a battle story with a big bow.
what it means: a safety built on a condition has a crack in it, and one act goes through when everything lines up behind it.
what a scholar hears: the Tripura story, told in the Shiva Purana's Rudra Samhita, gives Shiva the names Tripurantaka and Tripurari.

the year just walked and kept

sources.ref: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Yuddha Khanda (the three cities of Taraka's sons and their destruction)

notes: Confirm from the Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Yuddha Khanda: the brothers as sons of Taraka; Brahma refusing immortality; Maya building cities of gold (heaven), silver (sky) and iron (earth); destruction possible only when the cities align and by a single arrow. The specific interval of alignment given in some tellings was deliberately left out.

Chariot details (earth as chariot, sun and moon as wheels, Brahma as charioteer, Vedas as horses, a mountain as the bow, Vishnu as the arrow) follow the common telling; confirm the Shiva Purana's list. The mountain is commonly Meru; left unnamed here.
'Some tellings say he smiled and the cities burned': confirm this variant is attested (it is widely told); it is framed as a variant.
The brothers' names and Maya's later fate were left out to keep the day to one idea.
